topics.title: Equation of a Straight Line
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: understand the relationship between a linear equation y=mx + c and its graph. (k u)
determine the x and y intercepts of a given linear graph. (u s)
determine the gradient of a straight line. (u s)
state the gradient of a straight line when given the equation. (k u)
apply the relationship of gradients of parallel and perpendicular lines to determine the equation of a straight line. (k u s)

body.text: A boda boda rider in Mbarara charges UGX 2,000 to start a trip and UGX 1,000 for every kilometre. If you draw a graph of fare against distance, the points lie on a straight line. In Senior 1 you met the equation y = mx + c. In this topic you will use it to describe any straight line: how steep it is, where it crosses the axes, and how it relates to other lines.
Gradient: how steep a line is

The gradient of a line measures its steepness. It tells you how much y changes when x increases by 1. We find it by taking two points on the line. We divide the change in y (the rise) by the change in x (the run).

body.speech: m equals y two minus y one, over x two minus x one

items: A positive gradient means the line goes up from left to right.
A negative gradient means the line goes down from left to right.
A horizontal line, such as y = 7, has gradient 0.
A vertical line, such as x = 3, has no gradient, because the run is zero and we cannot divide by zero.

body.title: Find the gradient of a line through two points
steps: A line passes through A(1, 3) and B(4, 9).
Change in y = 9 − 3 = 6.
Change in x = 4 − 1 = 3.
Gradient m = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
For a line through P(−2, 5) and Q(2, −3): m = (−3 − 5) ÷ (2 − (−2)) = −8 ÷ 4 = −2. This line slopes downwards.

body.text: The equation y = mx + c and its graph
Every straight line that is not vertical has an equation of the form y = mx + c. The number m is the gradient. The number c is the y-intercept, the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis.

body.speech: y equals m x plus c

body.text: For the boda boda, let x be the distance in kilometres and y the fare in shillings. The fare rises by 1,000 for each kilometre, so m = 1,000. The starting charge is 2,000, so c = 2,000. Here the gradient is a rate of change: shillings per kilometre.

body.speech: y equals one thousand x plus two thousand

body.text: Reading the gradient from an equation
You can only read m and c straight from the equation when it is written as y = mx + c. If the equation looks different, first make y the subject.

body.title: State the gradient and y-intercept of 2y = 3 − x
steps: Divide every term by 2: y = 3/2 − x/2.
Rewrite in the order y = mx + c: y = −½x + 3/2.
The gradient is m = −½.
The y-intercept is c = 3/2, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 1.5).

body.text: Finding the x and y intercepts

The y-intercept is where the line meets the y-axis. Every point on the y-axis has x = 0. The x-intercept is where the line meets the x-axis. Every point on the x-axis has y = 0. Only two points are needed to draw a straight line, so the two intercepts give a quick way to draw it.

body.title: Find the intercepts of 3x + 2y = 12
steps: For the y-intercept, put x = 0: 2y = 12, so y = 6. The point is (0, 6).
For the x-intercept, put y = 0: 3x = 12, so x = 4. The point is (4, 0).
Plot (0, 6) and (4, 0) and join them with a ruler.
Gradient = (0 − 6) ÷ (4 − 0) = −3/2. This matches y = −3/2 x + 6 after making y the subject.

body.text: Finding the equation of a line

To write the equation of a line you need its gradient and one point on it. If you are given two points, find the gradient first. Then put one point into y = mx + c to find c. The form below gives the same answer.

body.speech: y minus y one equals m times, x minus x one

body.title: Find the equation of the line through (2, 5) and (6, 13)
steps: So y = 2x + c.
Put in the point (2, 5): 5 = 2 × 2 + c, so c = 1.
The equation is y = 2x + 1.
Check with the other point: 2 × 6 + 1 = 13. Correct.

body.text: Parallel lines never meet, like the two edges of a straight road. They have the same steepness, so they have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. When you multiply their gradients, the answer is −1. So if one line has gradient m, a line perpendicular to it has gradient −1/m.

body.speech: for parallel lines, m one equals m two. For perpendicular lines, m one times m two equals minus one

body.title: Find the line through (3, −1) perpendicular to y = 2x − 5
steps: The given line has gradient 2.
The perpendicular gradient is −1 ÷ 2 = −½. Check: 2 × (−½) = −1.
So y = −½x + c.
The equation is y = −½x + ½. Multiplying by 2 and rearranging gives x + 2y = 1.

body.title: The leaning ladder
body.text: Lean a metre rule or a straight stick against a wall. Place its foot 80 cm, then 50 cm, then 20 cm from the wall. Each time, measure how high up the wall the top reaches and work out height ÷ distance. This is the gradient of the stick. How do the angle and the gradient change as the foot moves closer to the wall? Then, on squared paper, draw a line and a second line at right angles to it. Find both gradients and multiply them. Try another pair. What do you notice?

Two boda boda riders in Gulu each draw a graph of fare against distance. One line is steeper. The other line crosses the y-axis higher up. For a short trip and for a long trip, which rider would you choose, and why?

Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x. In y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept; make y the subject before reading them. Put x = 0 to find the y-intercept and y = 0 to find the x-intercept. Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular gradients multiply to give −1.
